summary: Redwood team (AE + SE) walked Nimbus Health through the Console tracing, error analysis, and request logs UI focusing on debugging flows and compliance. questions: How long are request logs retained by default?
Can logs be exported to customer S3 or SIEM?
How do you redact PHI from request logs and traces?
What are latency implications of continuous tracing vs sampled tracing?
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-08
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Alec Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (CTO - Nimbus Health), Angela Ruiz (Dev Lead), Tom Wei (Security), Maya (SRE)

[00:00] Alec: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have a full house from Nimbus, appreciate the time. I'm Alec from Redwood, this is Priya, our solutions engineer, and we're going to walk through the Console tracing, error analysis, and request logs flows and show how you'd debug production issues.

[00:22] Samir: Thanks, Alec. Quick context — we're a health platform, mostly PHI in some flows, so HIPAA and auditability are big. We're evaluating hosted first but need to understand private options.

[00:35] Priya: Great, we'll highlight retention, KMS, and export options. We'll start in the Console — first panel is recent requests, per-route breakdowns, and per-model latency histograms.

[01:12] Priya: (screen share) you can see requests come in here, each row has a request id, route, model, tokens in/out, and a link to open the trace and full request log. I'll click one that errored.

[01:38] Angela: I see — is that request id correlated to our backend request ids? We want to join them in our logs.

[01:45] Priya: Yes, you can pass a client_request_id in the API and we persist it; the Console shows both Redwood request id and your client id so you can join. Sometimes the transcription in the exported CSV shows client r id as cl_id, we've seen that crop up in automated exports.

[02:10] Tom: What's the retention window for request logs by default?

[02:15] Priya: Defaults are 30 days for hosted, with 90/365 options for enterprise tiers. For Private you control retention. We also support exporting raw logs to a customer S3 or pushing to Splunk/Datadog via our export connector.

[02:48] Samir: We need 7 years for audit in certain cases — is that feasible?

[02:55] Alec: For long-term retention we typically do export to customer storage; storing 7 years in-hosted gets expensive and we recommend archiving to S3 with lifecycle policies. We'll include a note in the SOC2 pack about export patterns.

[03:22] Priya: Back to the trace — you can see the timeline with token generation spans, model server latencies, and any fallback routing. Errors show as red nodes, and expanding the node shows stderr or model-side errors, often truncated.

[03:48] Maya: Are stack traces preserved or are they sanitized? We need to know what might contain PHI.

[03:55] Priya: By default we redact obvious PII on stored request bodies if opt-in redaction is enabled. Detailed stack traces may be stored in logs depending on your settings — we can configure automatic redaction rules and also support on-write encryption with customer KMS so only you can decrypt the payloads.

[04:22] Tom: KMS — do you support bringing our own key / HSM?

[04:28] Alec: Yes, for Private and Dedicated we support customer-managed keys (AWS KMS, CloudHSM options). For hosted you can request a BYOK path; we'll need to go through the security gating. We'll attach the KMS whitepaper.

[04:52] Priya: Now the error analysis tab — it aggregates per-error signature, example requests, and stacks where available. You can search by model or route and create saved queries for recurring errors.

[05:20] Angela: Does the Console show inference-level logs like token-level timings?

[05:26] Priya: Yes, we capture token latency distribution and kernel-level timings in the performance profiling view for supported models — this helps diagnose whether slowdowns are model compute vs I/O. Note: token-level capture is sampling by default to avoid cost overhead; you can enable continuous profiling for a window during a POC.

[06:00] Samir: Sampling — how does that affect accuracy of the latency histograms?

[06:06] Priya: Sampling is probabilistic, typically 1-5% by default. It skews low-frequency anomalies minimally but for full fidelity we run a short continuous capture during an incident or POC. We'll show how to start a capture.

[06:28] Priya: (does capture demo) you can hit "Start trace capture" for a particular pool, set duration, and then we stream traces to the Console and to your export target.

[06:55] Speaker 1: (mumble) sorry little echo —

[07:02] Alec: No worries. Another important piece is correlating request logs to traces and to your backend traces. Each request has a trace id that can be passed into Redwood via header, and we instrument trace links you can click to open the full flame graph.

[07:30] Tom: For HIPAA we need strict access controls — who can see request bodies in Redwood Console?

[07:38] Priya: We have RBAC — roles like admin, read-only, support-access (audited). All accesses are logged. We can also disable Console access and only allow API + exports for customers who want no hosted UI access.

[07:58] Angela: How about masking PII in logs? Example: patient name in prompts.

[08:05] Priya: Two options: client-side redaction before sending, or server-side redaction rules (regex or ML-based redaction) applied at ingestion. For sensitive workloads customers often do both. We'll include the redaction guide in the follow-up.

[08:28] Samir: Performance — if we enable continuous tracing or increased logging, what's the token cost and latency impact?

[08:36] Priya: Logging itself is separate from per-token billing, but continuous trace capture increases IO and storage costs and can add a small latency overhead (tens of ms) in extreme cases. Our Optimize recommendations can suggest sampling rates and batching configs to reduce cost while keeping SLOs.

[09:05] Priya: Now switching to request logs view — here's a raw request, with headers, prompt, model, and response. You can expand and see alternative generations, rerank scores if you have reranking enabled.

[09:30] Angela: Can we redact before the log is persisted? We can't have PHI in raw storage.

[09:36] Priya: Yes, there's an ingestion pipeline hook and redaction can be applied server-side prior to persistence. For Private deployments you can enforce that policy via config.

[09:55] Samir: For the POC, the main success criteria are: average latency < 350ms p50 on our benchmark, under $0.0008 per token effective cost after batching, and full traceability for incident audits.

[10:14] Alec: Great, those are clear. We'll validate in POC. Priya will help set up the bench.

[10:22] Priya: A quick note on dedup & KV cache — prefix caching can reduce cost; we showed in another call how repetitive prompts get cache hits. If you pin model versions, cache warming strategies can further reduce p50.

[10:45] Tom: For exported logs, is there a field mapping doc? Our SIEM people need keys consistent with their parsers.

[10:52] Priya: Yes, we have a JSON schema for exports and a mapping config. We'll share the schema and a sample CSV.

[11:10] Alec: (recap) Next steps: we'll send SOC2/ISO + HIPAA notes, Priya will share the recording and deck, Samir to send sample workload and qps targets, and Tom to send KMS preferences. We'll aim to get the POC started next week pending procurement.

[11:40] Samir: Sounds good, thanks everyone.

[11:44] Angela: Thanks, helpful demo.

[11:48] Tom: One final Q: can we do a quick run of a failure scenario? Like model fallback to smaller model and how traces reflect it?

[11:56] Priya: Absolutely — quick demo: I'm going to simulate a capacity fallback by toggling the policy. You can see the trace shows two model spans — primary and fallback — along with a routing decision in the trace metadata. The error analysis groups fallback events so you can alert on them.

[12:30] Samir: That's perfect. We'll review and follow up on the action items.

[12:36] Alec: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the docs and get the POC planning thread started.

[12:40] (call ends)

Notes: transcript contains occasional mis-transcriptions (client r id sometimes appears as cl id, KV cache sometimes transcribed as K V cash), speaker 1 audio glitch around 06:55.
